added.change: **An MCP endpoint at `/mcp`,** so an AI assistant can read and write your cards, decks and collections through the same code the web interface runs. Mint a token for yourself at `/tokens`: it is shown once and stored only as a digest, so nobody can read it back out of the server. Every token can write, and anyone holding one can do anything to your cards that you can. Cards, decks, collections, saved decks and a collection's scheduling settings are writable; the schedule itself is not, so there is no way to make a card be forgotten, set its due date or suspend it. Nothing an assistant deletes is destroyed: it goes to the trash, and there is no tool that empties it. The endpoint is on by default and needs no configuration to reach from the same machine, but an instance served under a real hostname **must** name it in `[mcp].allowed_hosts` or every request is refused with nothing in the log to explain it -- the MCP SDK validates the `Host` header against a loopback-only default, as protection against a browser page driving a local MCP server by rebinding DNS at it.

**A trash.** Deleting a file, a folder or a whole collection moves it to `{data_dir}/trash/` instead of destroying it, and `/trash` lists what is in there and restores it. A deleted collection keeps its review history for as long as it is in the trash: card hashes are content addresses, so a restored folder finds its own rows again and its whole schedule comes back with nothing replayed.

breaking.change: **Deleting no longer takes effect immediately.** Anything deleted from My Cards goes to the trash and keeps its review rows until you empty it, and emptying the trash is now the only thing in hashcards that destroys anything -- including the review history of any collection in there, which is what still stops a collection recreated under an old name inheriting a stale schedule. Disk space is not reclaimed until you empty it. The refusal of a non-empty folder is gone with the same change: it existed because a misclick was unrecoverable, and it is not any more, so a collection full of topics can be deleted in one action.

changed.change: **One review database per user, instead of one per collection.** A collection's schedule lived in `{data_dir}/db/{id}.db`, a grain inherited from the CLI this server was forked from, where a collection was the directory you ran the tool in. Nothing about a multi-user server wanted it: `db/` was flat and shared, so which user owned a database could only be discovered by walking every tree and reading every `.hashcards.toml`; a folder deleted from outside the application orphaned its database for ever, with nothing able to collect it or even attribute it; the landing page opened one connection per collection on every request, and the startup sweep spawned a thread per database. Every row now carries the `collection_id` it belongs to, and one file holds everything one user has. Identical cards in two collections still keep two schedules — that is what two files necessarily meant, and it is now the primary key. Databases are opened with write-ahead logging where the filesystem allows it, so the stats page reading while a drill session writes no longer waits out a busy timeout; where it does not, hashcards logs a line and carries on in rollback-journal mode, because an optimisation must not refuse to start the server.

breaking.change: **Existing review databases are merged at first start, and the upgrade is one way.** Each user's per-collection databases are folded into one, in a single transaction per user, and the originals are moved — never deleted — into `{data_dir}/db/legacy/`. A user whose merge fails is refused with an error naming the startup log, and every other user is served: silently starting someone from an empty database is the one outcome this change exists to prevent. Downgrading afterwards fails *quietly* — an older binary looks for `db/{id}.db`, finds nothing, and creates empty per-collection databases with no error at all. To go back: stop the server, move `db/legacy/` back into `db/`, and delete the `db/{tree}.db` files. The originals are kept precisely so that this is possible, and are moved rather than left in place because an older binary writing into a file that has already been merged would have its reviews skipped by the next upgrade and lost without a word.

added.change: **Desired retention and the maximum interval are configurable, per instance and per collection.** Both were constants: `TARGET_RECALL = 0.9` and `MAX_INTERVAL = 256.0` days. Retention is the one FSRS number a person has an opinion about, because it names the trade the algorithm exists to make — raise it and every interval shortens, so you see more cards and remember more of them. The ceiling was doing more scheduling than anyone knew: a card known well enough for FSRS to ask for two years was silently handed back after eight and a half months, and nothing on screen said so. `[defaults]` now takes `desired_retention` (0.7 to 0.99) and `max_interval_days` (1 to 36500), and a collection's own `.hashcards.toml` may override either — retention is genuinely per-subject, since an exam in a fortnight and a language you intend to keep are not the same promise. Both default to the old constants, so no existing schedule moves. A value out of range in the instance config stops the server at startup, where it can be attributed; one in a collection's file is ignored with a warning and the collection still appears, because losing a collection from the landing page over a preference is the worse answer. The settings are resolved per review database rather than per session, so a deck drawing on several collections schedules each card by the collection that holds it — a card keeps exactly one schedule however it was reached. Jitter stays per instance: it spreads one person's review peaks across everything they study, so one collection deciding it alone would decide nothing. The uncapped interval is still recorded alongside the capped one, so raising the ceiling later does not have to recover a stability the ceiling threw away.

fixed.change: **The stylesheet is served from a path that names its own hash.** It was served `immutable` from `/style.css`, and `immutable` does not merely permit a cache to skip revalidation — it forbids it. So for a week after any deploy, a browser that had already fetched the stylesheet ran a week-old copy of it against freshly rendered HTML, and nothing shipped in between could be seen on that device at all. Two devices pointed at one server would disagree about the layout with no way to tell which was right. The path now carries sixteen hex characters of the hash of the bytes it serves, so a build that changes the stylesheet changes the URL that asks for it and `immutable` is honest. `/style.css` still answers, since a page cached from before this change still asks for it, but it now says `no-cache`: nothing may be kept against a name that does not describe its contents. `/script.js` and a collection's own `script.js` say the same, for the same reason — a script a week out of step with the HTML that loads it is the same bug, quieter.

**Every asset served `immutable` now comes from a path that names it, and every such path answers a revision it has never heard of.** The stylesheet was the loud case, but KaTeX, highlight.js and the fonts were served `immutable` from fixed paths too: bumping a vendored library left every browser that had fetched it running the old copy for a week, with no way to invalidate — the same bug, one asset class over. All of them now carry sixteen hex characters of the hash of what this build ships, and because the fonts are named by stylesheets rather than by HTML, both `style.css` and KaTeX's stylesheet have their `url()` references rewritten to carry that revision as they are served. The other half matters as much: HTML a browser already holds asks for the *previous* revision, and a 404 there is a page with no styling, no maths and no highlighting — strictly worse than the staleness being fixed. An unrecognised revision is therefore answered with the current bytes, marked `no-cache` so the client keeps nothing it cannot name. The old fixed paths still answer on the same terms, for pages rendered before any of this.

**A mistyped preference in a collection's `.hashcards.toml` no longer makes the collection disappear.** The override reader was careful to ignore a value out of range, but the file was parsed a second time — strictly — to read the `id`, so `desired_retention = "0.95"` was a parse error and the folder was skipped: the collection vanished from the landing page along with every review it had recorded. This was newly reachable, since per-collection scheduling is the first thing that invites anyone to hand-edit that file. Overrides are now read untyped and validated leniently, so a value of the wrong type is ignored with a warning exactly as an out-of-range one is. A file TOML cannot parse at all is not given up on either: the `id` is looked for by eye, since it is always one plain line and is the one thing that cannot be worked out again. Only a file with no readable `id` is skipped — and it has to be, because the alternative is minting a fresh id and writing over what you were in the middle of typing.

**End session is a line of text again, not a fifth grade button.** It was written to be one — `.end-link` sets no background, no border, and small muted type — but `.controls button` is a class and an element where `.end-link` is a class alone, so it was the more specific of the two and won every declaration they share. The way out of a session therefore rendered as a bordered 44px button directly under Forgot/Hard/Good/Easy, in a bar whose whole point is that it holds grades and nothing else. The grade rules now exclude it by name rather than being argued with.

added.change: **A card can be edited while you are drilling it.** A pencil sits beside the bookmark star once the answer is revealed, and saving lands back on the card, re-rendered. It was refused before, and had to be: a live session keys card identity in four places — the queue, where a card requeued by Forgot or Hard appears twice; the undo stack, which holds the performance to restore; the performance cache; and the per-card database routes that send a custom deck's grades to the collection the card actually belongs to — and an edit renames the hash all four are keyed by. The session now follows the card, so the grade after an edit lands on the card in front of you and the old card's schedule comes with it. The pencil appears only after the answer is shown: opening the editor earlier would put the answer in a textarea in front of a user still trying to recall it. A card the edit deleted leaves the queue and the undo stack — undoing back to a card that is in no file would offer something you could not edit, re-drill or reach again — and an edit that empties the queue finishes the session rather than leaving a live one with nothing in it. Every topic in a collection now carries an Edit link to its file in the in-app editor, pointing at the file the cards actually live in rather than at the topic's name, which a file's frontmatter can change without moving anything. The whole-file editor migrates a running session the same way. Deleting or renaming a collection is still refused while it is being drilled: a session cannot be re-keyed onto cards that are gone, and deleting a collection unlinks the database the session still holds open. The bookmark star's tooltip no longer says "for later editing": with editing one tap away, a bookmark means "save this for later" again.

changed.change: **Drill** on the collection list now starts the session. It used to open a topic picker whose own button also said "Drill", so studying a collection always cost two presses of the same word — and on a first visit the picker's answer was already the one you wanted, every topic with anything due pre-ticked. The one-tap start takes every topic and no limit; a collection's own page, now reached by its name, is where you go to drill part of one, or to look at its topics, stats, bookmarks and export.

The drill's bottom bar holds the grades and nothing else. Undo and Bookmark sat in it at the same weight as Forgot/Hard/Good/Easy, and on a phone the bar became a column where each of them was a full-width button — three ways to lose a session's place, all the size of the buttons pressed hundreds of times an hour. Undo is now a back-arrow in the top-left corner, Bookmark a star in the top-right, and End a quiet line under the grades. The theme switch, which floats in that top-right corner on every page, is hidden during a session: a drill is not where a theme gets chosen, and it would sit on the star.

"Deck" now means one thing. It named both a heading inside a collection's markdown and a saved cross-collection selection, to the point where the decks page had to define itself with a sentence using the word twice. The heading is a **topic**; a **deck** is only ever the saved selection. Saved decks are also no longer kept behind a "Manage Decks" button — they are drillable in exactly the way a collection is, so they are listed among the collections, tagged, with their own counts.

The collection list is one list again. Four full-width bars — sign-in, decks, sources, git — announced background details above it, each as loud as the thing the page is for. They are now one line of small links beside the title and one muted status line under it, and the collections are rows carrying the due count in the one colour on the page.

removed.change: **Remote sources are gone.** `[git]`, `[[source]]`/`[[hedgedoc]]` and the auto-commit of web edits are removed, and with them the `/sources` page, both background sync tasks and every outbound request except OIDC. They could not be edited: a save to a HedgeDoc-backed collection was overwritten on the next sync tick with no warning, and a commit into the git worktree was never pushed, so once the remote moved the branch had diverged and every later `git pull --ff-only` failed silently. A collection is now one thing — a top-level folder in your own card tree, discovered by reading the directory and identified by the stable id in its `.hashcards.toml` — so "a card can be edited" is a flat fact about the application rather than a property of where the card came from. Ownership is structural too: which tree a folder sits in is who owns it, so a collection nobody can reach stops being expressible. Three slug namespaces collapse to one, two database-naming schemes to one, and `{data_dir}/local` is renamed `{data_dir}/cards` now that there is no `{data_dir}/repo` for it to be named against. Review databases stay in `{data_dir}/db` under the names they already have, so no history moves. To bring markdown in, create a file in **My Cards** and paste the text into the editor, which previews through the production parser and validates images before saving. Nothing was deployed, so there is no migration: `[git]`, `[[source]]`, `[[hedgedoc]]` and `[[collection]]` are no longer accepted in `hashcards.toml`.

The notice about sessions a crash left open is now reported per review database rather than per URL slug, and the startup sweep that finds them walks every user's card tree. It used to iterate only the configured collections, which no longer exist; and two users who both call a collection "Spanish" slugify alike, so whichever of them opened the page first was shown the other's count.

fixed.change: Deleting or renaming a collection is no longer allowed out from under a running cross-collection deck. Sessions are keyed by URL slug and a saved deck has its own, so the guard that looked the *collection's* slug up in the session map never saw a deck session drawing on it: the collection went, taking the review database the session still held open, and every grade written afterwards landed in a file nothing could read back. A session is now found by asking what it actually loaded.
The session-completed screen no longer navigates away on a five-second timer. It is the one page in a session a user might want to sit and read.

A running drill belongs to the user who started it. Sessions were filed under the URL slug alone, and a collection is now a folder in its owner's card tree, so two users each owning a "Spanish" both address it as `Spanish` — whoever asked second was shown the other's live card, and could Reveal, grade, Undo and End it, writing reviews into a database that was never theirs. The same slug on the collection list offered a stranger's session to Resume. Sessions are now keyed by owner as well as slug.

A card drilled inside a deck can be edited and shows its images. The pencil and the media URLs both name the slug the session is filed under, which for a saved deck is the deck's own slug and names no collection at all: the editor answered "Unknown collection: deck-..." with a 500, and every image in the session 404'd. The editor now looks through a deck to the member collection that actually holds the card — which is also the only way a deck spanning several collections could name the right one — and returns to the drill it was opened from. Each session records the home collection of every card it holds, not only the ones drawing on more than one collection.

An edit that makes a card byte-identical to another card the session is already drilling no longer corrupts the survivor's schedule. The database declines that rename — the target has its own history, and neither row may be destroyed — but the session's performance cache took the rename anyway, so the next grade of the surviving card computed its stability, difficulty and interval from the edited-away card's history. The cache now keeps what the database kept.

A deck whose counts cannot be worked out is still listed. It was logged and dropped, so a deck whose member collection had stopped loading — one missing image is enough — vanished from the one page that lists it, with nothing on screen to say anything was wrong. It now appears, says "Counts unavailable", and explains itself when opened.

A card tree is named for its owner's email *and* eight characters of its hash. Slugifying alone is not injective — every character outside `[A-Za-z0-9._-]` becomes `-`, so `me+work@example.com` and `me-work@example.com` named one folder — and which tree a collection sits in is who owns it, so two OIDC identities would have shared every collection, every file and every review database. Nothing was deployed, so there is no migration; a tree left over from a local run is renamed by hand or created afresh.

A term-definition pair whose `T:` or `D:` spans several lines no longer produces a card that reads as a copy of its twin. The body used to be interpolated into the `Define:` or `Term for:` prompt, where markdown folded its first line into the prompt and rendered the rest as a sibling block, stranding the answer underneath and leaving nothing to recall. The prompt now keeps its own line and the body stays a block — which is what `Q:` followed by those lines parses to, so the shorthand and the explicit form still share a hash. A one-line term or definition is unchanged and stays inline, so existing cards keep their history.
The editor preview no longer says "1 cards". The count and the noun it counts now agree in number, as they already did in the collection browser's duplicates notice.

Cloze cards render in the editor preview the way they do in a drill. The preview drew its cards without the `rich-text` class every rule in the stylesheet is scoped to, so the blank came out as literal dots instead of a grey box and the revealed word carried no highlight, making the back look like an unchanged copy of the front. Images, tables, code blocks, blockquotes and list indentation were unstyled there for the same reason.

added.change: Cards can now be written in hashcards itself. **My Cards** (`/files`) is a folder tree kept at `{data_dir}/local/{user}` that only its owner writes to, with a file manager for creating, renaming and deleting folders and files, and a Markdown editor whose buttons insert Q/A, cloze, term, separator, LaTeX and image skeletons at the caret. It sits outside `{data_dir}/repo` deliberately: `clone_or_pull` hard-updates that directory and source sync overwrites the files it owns, so a separate root makes "sync cannot clobber your writing" a property of the layout rather than a rule to remember. Each top-level folder is a collection, discovered rather than configured, and carries a `.hashcards.toml` holding a stable id — review databases are named from that id rather than from the slug, so renaming a folder keeps its history instead of silently orphaning the database. Saving reuses the card editor's atomic write, revert and hash migration, so a buffer that does not parse never survives on disk and a reworded card keeps its schedule; a file that no longer parses on disk can still be repaired in the editor, since the history it carries forward is a matter of what the old content held, not a precondition for saving. A folder may not take the URL slug of a collection or source that already exists — routing prefers those, so it would be unreachable — and one that comes to collide later is dropped from the collection list with a warning rather than stopping the server. That check covers every way a top-level folder can come into being, a file created under a parent that does not exist yet included, since a folder dropped from the list says so only in the log. Deleting an emptied collection folder deletes its review database too, instead of orphaning it under a name nothing can address again — and only once the folder itself is gone, so a removal that fails leaves the history it still needs. Saving is refused while a drill session is running on the collection, exactly as editing a single card is: rewriting card hashes under a live session strands the grades it is about to write. It is also refused when the buffer names an image that is not there, which would otherwise fail the collection's media validation and take its page, deck tree, stats and landing count down together. A refused save answers with the editor over the text that was submitted rather than redirecting to a page that re-reads the file from disk, so a buffer is never thrown away for one bad card. Local collections can be put in custom decks like any other. A file sitting directly in the card folder belongs to no collection, so it is shown as plain text rather than offered an editor that could neither save it nor draw its images, and one can no longer be created there at all. Deleting or renaming is refused while a drill session is running on the collection, for the same reason saving is: deleting a collection unlinks the database the session still holds open, and every grade it writes after that goes to a file nothing can read back. A folder inside a collection may not be called `media` — that is where pasted images are kept, so the file manager hides it and does not count it when deciding whether a collection is empty, and a folder of the user's own under that name would be invisible to both, taking the decks inside it with the collection on a single click of Delete; one made by hand before the name was reserved is still there, so deleting a collection now says where those files are rather than removing them unseen. Client paths are normalized once, when they are resolved, so that where a file is and which collection owns it can no longer be answered differently: `./Spanish` used to resolve to the collection folder while a raw split called it nested, deleting it without its review database and slipping past the active-session guard. Every handler in the file manager and the editor does its filesystem and SQLite work off the async executor.

Images can be pasted into a card. Ctrl+V in the editor uploads the clipboard image to `{Collection}/media/`, names it after a hash of its own bytes — one file however often the same screenshot is pasted, and no filename from a screenshot tool ever reaching disk — and writes a collection-relative `![](@/media/...)` reference at the caret, which resolves identically for a deck at a collection's root and one nested three folders down. PNG, JPEG, GIF and WebP up to 10 MB, the format read from the bytes rather than the name, and every one of them served back with its own content type rather than as a download; SVG is refused, being script-bearing markup served inline from the app's own origin. The `media` folder is storage rather than tree: the file manager hides it, and a collection whose decks are gone still counts as empty. The toolbar's Image button no longer inserts `![](image.png)` — a reference to a file that is never there fails the collection's media validation and takes its whole page down — and points at the paste path instead.

The file manager and the editor are drawn in the house identity like every other page: the tree is one bordered surface of rows with the collection in semibold and its actions grouped to the right, a folder's new-file and new-folder buttons share one name field, and the editor is two panes of equal height with the parse preview in a surface of its own. They previously carried ten lines of ad-hoc CSS appended after the responsive layer, with literal colours and no token in sight, and the editor was not in the page frame at all.

The editor previews as you type, running the buffer through the production parser rather than a JavaScript approximation, and reporting either the parsed cards or the parse error with its line number. An approximation could render a card hashcards cannot actually read, which is the one thing the preview exists to rule out. Duplicate cards are reported too.

A link to a Markdown file in a git repository can be added as a source, exactly like a HedgeDoc note. GitHub `/blob/`, GitLab `/-/blob/`, Gitea and Forgejo `/src/branch/` URLs are rewritten to their raw endpoints, and any URL already ending in `.md` is fetched as-is, except under `/s/`, which is HedgeDoc's own published-note shape and nothing else's — a note alias is free-form and may well end in `.md`. Anything else stays a HedgeDoc note. Only the step that builds the fetch URL differs, so adding, syncing, deleting and slugging are shared with HedgeDoc sources.

changed.change: `[[hedgedoc]]` config entries are now `[[source]]`, since a GitHub URL under a `hedgedoc` heading reads as a mistake. The old spelling still parses, so existing configs keep working; entries written back by the web interface use the new one, and the old array is removed when they are, because entries in both places would load every source twice.

`/hedgedoc` is now `/sources` and permanently redirects, so existing bookmarks keep working. The page gains a Kind column, whose badge is derived from the same URL logic that chooses where the markdown is fetched from, and offers a starter card template for copying into a note, a repository or a local file, both drawn with the shared tokens rather than left as browser defaults. Copying selects the template and says to press Ctrl+C where the clipboard API is not available — it is absent outside a secure context, so over plain HTTP on a LAN address the button used to throw and do nothing.

added.change: A theme switch sits in the top-right corner of every page. It follows the system preference until it is pressed and remembers the choice in `localStorage` from then on; the choice is applied by a small inline script before the first paint, so a stored theme does not flash the other one on every load. The button is rendered hidden and revealed by `script.js`, since without script it could neither remember a choice nor label itself — and it names where it goes rather than where it is.

changed.change: The interface is restyled to the corporate identity shared with Vestigo and engram: one palette of named tokens, a warm paper light theme and a cool ink dark theme that follows the system preference, Inter and JetBrains Mono served from the binary, and one button, field, table and notice shared by every page. The stylesheet was previously a set of per-page rules written against hard-coded greys, so pages built later — Decks, HedgeDoc sources, the stats charts — arrived with browser-default fieldsets and submit buttons, and nothing had a dark theme at all. `vendor/highlightjs` ships the light GitHub theme only, so its code colours are restated for dark here rather than a second theme being vendored.

The stylesheet, its fonts and the vendored KaTeX and highlight.js assets are served outside the OIDC gate. They hold nothing about anyone's cards, and the pages shown to a user who is not logged in — the login page and the "session expired" page — link them, so under `[oidc]` exactly those pages were the ones whose stylesheet redirected to `/auth/login` and arrived unstyled.

On the stats page a day with reviews on it is now drawn at least one percent high, and a day with none is drawn as nothing. Days rounding below one percent of the busiest day vanished, while the stylesheet's one-pixel floor drew a line across every empty day — so a chart of a quiet month read as a dashed rule rather than as zero.

fixed.change: The server now creates `data_dir` and its `db/` and `hedgedoc/` subdirectories at startup, and refuses to start with a message naming the directory when it cannot. Only the git-mode directories were created before, and only when `[git]` was configured, so a `data_dir` the server could not write went unnoticed until the first write — adding a HedgeDoc note, possibly many restarts later — which failed with a bare "I/O error: Permission denied (os error 13)" naming no path at all. Every directory the server creates now reports its own path and role on failure. The shipped example points `data_dir` at `/var/lib/hashcards`, which is root-owned unless the systemd unit declares `StateDirectory=hashcards`; the README and the example config now say so and show the unit file.

Login no longer fails with "OIDC provider did not return an email claim" against providers that do not put `email` in the ID token. OpenID Connect Core 5.4 returns the `email` scope's claims from the UserInfo endpoint in the authorization code flow, and carrying them in the ID token as well is the provider's option — Nextcloud's OIDC app does not. hashcards now reads the ID token, falls back to UserInfo, and finally to the `sub` claim, which every ID token carries and whose signature is already verified. The UserInfo request is best-effort: a provider without the endpoint, or one that fails the request, no longer turns a valid login into an error. `[oidc].scopes` accordingly need only include `openid`; a deployment whose provider sends no email at all writes the subject in `owner` instead.

OIDC discovery now follows redirects that stay on the issuer's own origin, so Nextcloud works again. Nextcloud serves its discovery document at `/index.php/.well-known/openid-configuration` and redirects the standard `/.well-known/openid-configuration` there, while the document declares the bare host as its issuer — so with redirects refused outright there was no `issuer_url` that worked: the bare host failed on the 301, and the `/index.php` form failed the issuer check that OpenID Connect Discovery requires. Redirects that leave the origin are still refused, since following one would hand a third-party host the request and, at the token endpoint, the client credentials. `hashcards.example.toml` documented the wrong `issuer_url` for Nextcloud and now explains how to read the right one out of the discovery document.

added.change: The collection page now reports byte-identical duplicate cards, naming both file locations. Duplicates are deduplicated at load time, so one copy is dropped and only the other carries review history; this was previously only warned about on the CLI's stderr.

New route `GET /collection/{slug}/export` returns a collection as JSON — every card, its scheduling state, and the full review history — as a file download, gated to the collection's owner. The markdown lives in git but the review databases do not, and under `[oidc]` a user has no filesystem access, so this is their only route to their own history. It is linked from the collection page, next to Stats.

changed.change: The project is now `hashcards-web`: a web server rather than the CLI it was forked from. The package, binary, release artifacts and documentation are renamed; the Apache-2.0 licence and all upstream copyright headers are unchanged. On-disk `hashcards.toml` and `hashcards.db` keep their names, so existing deployments are unaffected — but the binary is now `hashcards-web`, so anyone installed under the old name must reinstall.

The `drill`, `check`, `stats`, `orphans` and `export` subcommands are removed, along with the drill web server they drove. The binary now takes a single optional `--config`, defaulting to `hashcards.toml` in the current directory, and fails with a clear message when there is no configuration file.

`hashcards.example.toml` now documents the `[oidc]` section, the `owner` key on `[[collection]]`/`[[hedgedoc]]`/`[[deck]]` entries, and the `[[deck]]` table itself — all of which shipped in 0.4.2 but were only described in the README. The README is rewritten around the server, and the stale `SPEC.md`, `ROADMAP.md`, `PLAN.md` and `docs/superpowers/plans/` ledgers, which describe already-landed work in terms of deleted code, are removed.

fixed.change: A KaTeX macro containing an apostrophe — `\text{don't}`, say — no longer breaks a collection's `script.js`. Macros were pasted into single-quoted JavaScript literals with only backslashes, backticks and dollar signs escaped, so an apostrophe closed the literal early and killed every script on the page; a crafted `macros.tex` could inject arbitrary JavaScript that way. The macro map is now emitted as JSON.

The duplicate-card notice on the collection page no longer shows the server's absolute path to each file, which under `[oidc]` was leaking the deployment's directory layout to users with no filesystem access. Locations are now relative to the collection, and the notice reads correctly when there is exactly one duplicate.

`make example` works on a fresh clone again: `example/hashcards.toml` was matched by the root `.gitignore` rule for `hashcards.toml` and so was never committed, making the target fail with "Config file not found".

removed.change: The dead `Shutdown` action, left over from the drill server: it was still accepted from form input but the server-mode handler discarded it, so it silently did nothing or produced a nonsensical "press End before shutting down" message.

The two ways to start the server without a configuration file — passing collection directories positionally, and the config-free HedgeDoc-only mode that ran out of a temporary directory — are gone. Both hardcoded `oidc: None`, so each was an unauthenticated bypass of the access control the rest of the server enforces. `create_minimal_config`, which wrote a config file on the first HedgeDoc add, goes with them.

added.change: Optional OIDC authentication for `serve` mode: an `[oidc]` config section gates every route except `/auth/*` behind login (validated against Nextcloud), and each `[[collection]]`/`[[hedgedoc]]` entry declares an `owner` (matched against the OIDC `email` claim) so each user sees only their own collections. Sessions are stateless signed cookies; no server-side session store. Absent `[oidc]`, `serve` behaves exactly as before. `drill` mode is unaffected. In-browser edit commits are attributed to the logged-in user when OIDC is on.

Decks can now be assembled across collections: a `[[deck]]` entry (or the new `/decks` page) names a selection of decks drawn from any of your collections and drills them as one session. A deck owns no cards and no database — each review is routed back to the database of the collection its card came from, so a card included in several decks keeps exactly one schedule instead of becoming due twice on schedules that drift apart. Deleting a deck removes only the selection; cards and review history are untouched. With `[oidc]` configured, a deck is visible only to its owner and may only include collections that owner holds.

fixed.change: An `[oidc].session_secret` shorter than 32 bytes is now rejected at config load with a clear message instead of panicking at startup, and a collection or HedgeDoc entry that declares an `owner` without an `[oidc]` section is rejected too — previously it loaded cleanly and then 404'd for everyone, since nobody is ever logged in to match the owner.

changed.change: Each `[[hedgedoc]]` note is now a collection of its own rather than being grouped with every other note on the same HedgeDoc host. Slugs, note directories and review databases are keyed by (note URL, owner), so several users can take notes from one shared HedgeDoc instance — including the same note — without sharing a collection. Deleting a note removes only that note's own directory; its review database is kept as before. The HedgeDoc manage page lists one row per note and the landing page shows each note under its own title.

security.change: Fixed cross-user data exposure in HedgeDoc sources: `[[hedgedoc]]` entries were grouped by HedgeDoc host and took the owner of whichever entry was configured first, so on a shared HedgeDoc instance one user's note was served inside another user's collection — and the next add or delete rewrote the config file with the wrong owner recorded. Notes are no longer grouped, so an entry can never inherit another entry's owner.

Fixed an open redirect in the OIDC login flow: `return_to` is taken from the query string and is now required to be a path on this server, so a crafted login link can no longer bounce a user to an attacker's page immediately after a genuine login.

The OIDC session and login-flow cookies are now marked `Secure` when `external_url` is HTTPS, so a session credential can never ride a plaintext request. The session cookie also carries an explicit 30-day lifetime; without one it was a browser-session cookie that logged users out on every browser restart, contradicting the documented sliding session.

`/auth/logout` is now a POST (with a Log out button on the landing page) rather than a GET, so a third-party page can no longer log a user out by embedding the URL. A manual HedgeDoc sync now re-fetches only the caller's own notes instead of every user's, and its error messages no longer name other users' note URLs.
`[[hedgedoc]]` owners are now lowercased like collection owners, so a config written with mixed case matches the OIDC email claim as documented instead of making the owner's own notes unreachable.

A `[[hedgedoc]]` entry's `owner` now survives the config rewrite that follows adding or deleting a note. It was being dropped, which left a config that `[oidc]` validation rejects on the next startup, and would have re-keyed every note onto a fresh, empty review database.

An unauthenticated non-GET request now returns 401 with a "session expired" page instead of a redirect. A redirect is a 303, which replays the request as a GET of a POST-only path — a 405 with the submitted form data silently discarded. An expired or malformed login-flow cookie is also cleared from the browser now rather than left until its own expiry.

fixed.change: Fixed four Windows-only test failures surfaced by the Windows CI job: a collection path with a root but no drive prefix (e.g. `/etc`) is now rejected as absolute on every platform, not just Unix, closing a directory-traversal check that Windows' path-joining rules could otherwise bypass. A git-backed edit test no longer canonicalizes its temp path before handing it to `git clone`, which misread Windows' `\\?\` verbatim-path prefix as a UNC hostname. A double-quote-in-filename attribute-escaping test is now skipped on Windows, where filesystems refuse to create such a file in the first place.

security.change: Updated the `h2` dependency to 0.4.19, fixing RUSTSEC-2026-0258 (unbounded empty DATA frames).

breaking.change: Cloze card hashes are now derived from the card's text, the deleted substring, and an occurrence index, instead of the deletion's raw byte offsets. Card identity no longer depends on CPU endianness or pointer width, so a hashcards.db can move between machines. There is no automatic upgrade path: a database written by an older version keeps its old cloze hashes, which this version sees as orphans (visible to the orphans command) while the cloze cards themselves start fresh. (BUG-27)

fixed.change: Serve mode no longer deadlocks when a grade is submitted while the idle-session sweep or the collection list is running. The three code paths took the session map lock and a session's own lock in opposite orders; with no lock timeout this hung the server outright.

A line beginning with `D:` inside an answer is now ordinary text again. The new term/definition shorthand treated `D:` as a tag wherever it appeared, so an answer such as "D: dominant allele shown" failed the entire collection load. `D:` is a tag only directly below a `T:` line.

A line such as ```` ```code``` ```` no longer opens a code fence that is never closed, which silently swallowed every card below it in the file. A backtick fence's info string may not itself contain backticks.

A markdown link whose text contains brackets, for example `[the [inner] docs](url)`, no longer fails the deck with "Nested cloze brackets". Link labels may contain balanced brackets and are left to the link.
A cloze card with a malformed deletion range now reports a clear error instead of panicking while rendering.

Editing a card in the browser now keeps its review history when the edit adds a line above the card's own `Q:`. The new card was previously matched by its exact starting line, so shifting it down orphaned its history while still reporting "Card saved."

A browser edit's hash migration now runs in a single transaction, and an edit that makes a card identical to an existing one is reported instead of failing with a server error part-way through. Previously such an edit left the file saved, the database half-migrated and the working tree dirty.
Two Undo requests arriving together (a double click, or key auto-repeat) now void one review instead of two. Undo carries the review it means to void, the same guard grades already had.

Sessions left open by a crash or restart are now closed once, when the server starts, instead of on every visit to a collection, and only when they have been silent for over an hour. Sessions carry a heartbeat that the owning process stamps as it works, so a session still running in a concurrent `drill` — which shares the same database file — is no longer stamped as ended and left appending reviews to a row claiming to have finished. A session is also marked closed explicitly rather than inferred from its end time matching its start time, so one whose reviews were all undone is no longer re-reported on every sweep, forever. This adds schema version 7; existing databases are migrated in place on first open.

Database connections now wait for a lock held by another connection rather than failing immediately, and the drill stats page is rendered off the async runtime. Opening `/stats` while a grade was being written could return a server error.

Stats now count due cards from the parsed collection rather than the card table, which nothing populates before a collection's first drill. A collection that had never been drilled reported no cards due at all, and the due forecast counted orphaned rows that the per-deck column did not, so the two halves of the page disagreed.

Session completion stats are now computed from the session's persisted reviews: distinct cards and total reviews (including repeats) are reported separately, and the slowest-card row shows the card's question preview instead of its deck name. (BUG-13)
Per-card review timing now starts when the card is first displayed instead of when the answer is revealed, so recorded durations and pace stats include recall time. (BUG-14)

A second Ctrl+C during shutdown now stops hashcards immediately (exit code 130), and both drill and serve modes shut down gracefully on SIGTERM. Previously catching the first Ctrl+C replaced the default signal handling, so if shutdown stalled on an open client connection the process could only be stopped with SIGKILL. (BUG-52)

Interrupting a drill with Ctrl+C now exits cleanly: the session is closed, a summary of the saved reviews is printed, and the exit code is 0. Reviews are written to the database as they happen, so an interrupted session loses nothing. Previously the command exited with the error "Session interrupted before completion". (BUG-10)
Re-bookmarking a card during drilling (pressing `b` on an already-bookmarked card) no longer erases the bookmark's note or resets its creation time. (BUG-07)

Landing-page card counts now refresh when a drill session finishes or is ended, and on loading the landing page when the cached counts are older than the sync poll interval. Previously they went stale until the next sync or Home action. (BUG-45)

Serve-mode drill sessions idle for longer than a configurable timeout (`session_timeout_minutes`, default 24 hours) are now evicted and their database session rows closed; previously abandoned sessions lived forever and their session rows stayed open. Serve mode's single-user semantics are now documented in the README. (BUG-08)
Serve mode now runs collection parsing and database work on a blocking thread pool instead of the async runtime, so one slow request no longer stalls every other request. (BUG-44)

Serve mode now detects URL slug collisions between collections (e.g. paths `a/b` and `a-b`, or a configured collection shadowing a HedgeDoc source) at config load, at server startup, and when adding a HedgeDoc source, failing with a message naming both colliding collections. The startup check also covers sources configured in the config file and two source URLs that reduce to the same slug, neither of which was validated before. Previously one collection was silently routed to the other's database. (BUG-43)

HedgeDoc sources that fail to initialize at server startup (for example while the HedgeDoc instance is unreachable) are no longer silently dropped from the configuration. They now appear with an "Error" status, are retried on every sync, and are only removed when explicitly deleted. (BUG-40)

Deleting a HedgeDoc source now also deletes its downloaded note files from disk. The review database is deliberately kept so review history survives re-adding the source; the confirmation message states exactly what was deleted and what was kept. (BUG-42)

Adding and deleting HedgeDoc sources is now atomic: the duplicate check, the in-memory change, and the config-file write happen under a single lock, so concurrent add/delete requests can no longer lose configured sources. Failures are reported to the user instead of only being logged. (BUG-39)

HedgeDoc note filenames now include a short hash of the note ID, so two notes whose IDs differ only in special characters no longer overwrite each other's files. Old-format files are cleaned up automatically on the next sync. (BUG-41)

HedgeDoc URLs are now validated when a source is added: non-HTTPS or malformed URLs are rejected immediately with an error message instead of being persisted and showing a permanent "Error" status. (BUG-38)

When a cloze card is edited in the browser, review history now follows each deletion by its content instead of its position in the document. Reordering or removing a deletion no longer transplants history onto the wrong sibling card; cards that cannot be matched unambiguously start fresh, and the save notice says how many. (BUG-35)

Editing a one-line card (such as a single-line `C:` cloze) in the browser no longer duplicates it: the card's own first line is no longer mistaken for the end of its own block, so the edit replaces the line instead of being inserted above it.

The in-browser card editor now re-checks the source file's modification time immediately before atomically replacing it, so a concurrent change on disk is never silently overwritten. If reverting a rejected edit fails, the editor now reports that the file may be inconsistent instead of silently ignoring the failure. (BUG-36)

In serve mode, an error while rendering a card or handling an action no longer destroys the running drill session. The session now stays in place behind a per-collection lock, so after a transient error the same card is shown again and progress is kept.

Holding down a grading key or double-submitting a grade no longer grades several cards in a row: key auto-repeat is ignored in the browser, and the server ignores a grade for a card that is no longer current, showing a notice instead.
A grade submitted without a revealed answer (for example from a stale browser page) is no longer silently ignored: the page now shows a notice explaining that the grade was not counted.
Undoing after a session has finished now reopens the session's database row, so reviews made after the undo are attached to an open session instead of one that still claims to be closed.

Grading and undoing now commit to the database before changing the in-memory session. Previously a failed database write during a grade silently discarded the card (unrecorded and not undoable), and a failed write during undo could duplicate the card in the queue.
Pressing Shutdown before the drill session is finished now shows a message explaining that the session is still in progress, instead of silently doing nothing.

Byte-identical duplicate cards no longer disappear silently: collection loading keeps one copy and prints a warning naming both file locations, and drilling proceeds normally. Duplicates can no longer abort drill startup.
The collection browse page now reports database errors instead of silently displaying a bookmark count of zero.
HedgeDoc shared/published notes (URLs with a `/s/` path prefix) can now be registered as sources. Previously the `/download` URL was constructed incorrectly, causing fetches to fail.

HedgeDoc notes whose permission level prevents anonymous download (e.g. "Locked" or "Protected") now show an "Error" status with a descriptive message instead of silently reporting "OK" while storing an HTML page as markdown (yielding zero cards).

Ending a session before revealing or grading any card no longer shows nonsense statistics (0 cards reviewed over the whole server uptime); the completion page now simply reports that no cards were reviewed.
The drill-mode error page now returns HTTP 500 instead of 200, is styled, and has a link back to the session.
Starting a drill with no decks selected no longer silently drills the entire collection; it now shows "Select at least one deck."

Errors in web actions are no longer silently swallowed: failed grades and undos, bookmark removal and note saving, manual git sync, and all HedgeDoc add/delete/sync failures now show an error banner instead of redirecting as if they had succeeded.
Malformed lines in `macros.tex` (lines without a space between the macro name and its definition) are now reported as warnings with their line number instead of being silently ignored.

Removed panics reachable from web request handlers: an empty card queue and a premature completion-page request now render an error page instead of crashing the server; internal parser and grade-action inconsistencies, system-clock errors, and Ctrl+C handler failures are reported as errors instead of panicking.
Session and sync state locks no longer use `.lock().unwrap()`: a panic in one request can no longer poison the locks and cascade into crashes of every subsequent request.
An empty cloze deletion (`[]`) now produces a clear parse error with the file and line, instead of crashing the parser (debug builds) or silently corrupting cloze positions (release builds). (BUG-16)

Nested cloze brackets (`[[a]]`) and cloze deletions left open at the end of a line or file now produce clear parse errors with the file and line, instead of silently dropping brackets or reporting a misleading "must contain at least one cloze deletion" message. (BUG-19)

Markdown links (`[text](url)`) inside cloze cards are no longer misparsed as cloze deletions; they are passed through to Markdown like image syntax. The bracket escape rules are now documented in the README. (BUG-17)
`Q:`, `A:`, `C:`, and `---` lines inside fenced code blocks (``` or ~~~) are now treated as literal text instead of card syntax, so cards containing code samples parse correctly. (BUG-18)
Line numbers in parse errors, media errors, and the JSON export are no longer offset by the length of a file's TOML frontmatter; they now refer to real file lines. (BUG-20)

Frontmatter and file-read errors now name the file they came from; I/O, database, path, UTF-8, and JSON errors are rendered as human-readable messages instead of debug dumps; and parse errors no longer carry a redundant "Parse error:" prefix. (BUG-21)

Cloze deletion positions are documented as byte offsets (they were previously described as character positions, including in the JSON export), and a non-ASCII cloze round-trip test now pins this behavior. (BUG-26)

Cloze cards whose text literally contains the string `CLOZE_DELETION` no longer render that text as a spurious cloze blank. The internal placeholder is now generated per render and checked against the card text.
Cards no longer stay permanently invisible when the KaTeX script fails to load or math rendering throws: card content visibility is now restored even when rendering fails.
The error message for an invalid grade string now includes the offending value instead of the literal text `{value}`. (BUG-29)
A system clock rollback (a last-review timestamp in the future) no longer corrupts scheduling: negative elapsed time is clamped to zero, preventing NaN stability and intervals. (BUG-28)
Corrected documentation for `interval_raw` (card performance and JSON export): the value is in days, not hours. (BUG-30)

Deleting a card (e.g. via the orphans command) is now a single atomic statement relying on the database's foreign-key cascade. Previously the card's reviews were deleted in a separate step, so an interruption could erase review history while leaving the card in place. Note that card deletion permanently removes the card's review history and bookmarks; unlike undo, it does not keep a voided audit trail. (BUG-31)

Review lookups by card, by session, and by day are now backed by database indexes (including a generated per-day date column), so daily review counts and session stats no longer scan the whole reviews table. (BUG-33)

Loading a collection page no longer renders a session a concurrent request just ended (via Home, or idle eviction) as if it were still live. The GET path lacked the same "was this session removed from under me" check the drill actions already had, so it could go on stamping heartbeats and per-card timers on a session whose database row was already closed.

Saving a card edit no longer reports "could not be matched to their previous review history" for a card that simply had no prior review history to begin with (for example, a newly added card). That message is now reserved for true collisions, where the edited card became byte-identical to another card that already has its own history.
Loading a collection page now stamps the session heartbeat once per request instead of twice.

The startup sweep that closes dangling sessions now checks every collection's database concurrently instead of one after another, so server startup no longer slows down in proportion to how many collections are configured.

security.change: The URL of an audio media reference is now HTML-escaped before being embedded in the audio element, alongside its title. Percent-encoding leaves the double-quote character intact, so a media file whose name contained a quote could close the `src` attribute and inject arbitrary attributes into the page.

`hashcards stats --format html` now writes to a randomly named, owner-only file instead of a fixed path in the shared temporary directory. The old fixed name let any other local user pre-create it as a symlink and have a file the invoking user can write truncated, and left review statistics world-readable at a guessable path.
Titles of audio media references are now HTML-escaped before being embedded in the audio element, preventing HTML injection through a crafted markdown title.

HedgeDoc source URLs are now validated at storage time (well-formed HTTPS only) and re-checked at render time, so a link with an unsafe scheme such as `javascript:` can never be stored or rendered as a clickable link.

Symlinked directories inside a collection can no longer be used to serve files from outside the collection root: media paths are now canonicalized and must resolve inside the (canonicalized) collection directory, in both the file-serving endpoint and collection-relative (`@/`) media resolution (BUG-46).

The server now binds to 127.0.0.1 by default instead of 0.0.0.0. Listening on all interfaces requires an explicit opt-in (`host = "0.0.0.0"` in the config, or `--host 0.0.0.0`); the documentation now states that hashcards has no authentication (BUG-47).

Collection `path` entries in the configuration file are now validated at load time: absolute paths and paths containing `..` are rejected with a clear error, so a collection can no longer point outside the data directory. A relative collection directory passed to the media loader now produces an error instead of a panic (BUG-48).

added.change: Stats page: due forecast for the next 30 days, reviews per day over the last 90 days, grade distribution, retention estimate, and per-deck due/total counts. Available at `/collection/{slug}/stats` in serve mode and `/stats` while drilling; `hashcards stats` now renders the page to a file and opens it in the browser, replacing the unimplemented `--format html` stub. (FEAT-02)

The drill progress bar now has a numeric counter: "7 of 20 (+3 repeats)". The bar advances when a card is graded for the first time; cards re-queued by Forgot/Hard are tallied in the repeats counter instead of silently stalling the bar. Undo rolls the counter back. (FEAT-08)

Session resume: the collection list now shows "Resume session (N cards remaining)" for a running drill session, and starting a new drill no longer silently discards an unfinished one. Session rows left open by a crash or restart are closed and reported on the collection page; every review made before the interruption is kept. (FEAT-03)

In-browser edits in a git-backed collection are now committed automatically (message: `hashcards: web edit of <file>`, author configurable via `commit_author_name` / `commit_author_email` in the `[git]` config section). Every web edit thus gets versioned card history for free, and background git sync no longer breaks on a dirty working tree. Pull failures during manual sync are now reported in the browser instead of only being logged. (FEAT-04, BUG-34)

Flash messages: actions in the drill and serve web interfaces now show one-shot success/error banners (dismissible) instead of failing or succeeding silently. The message travels as query parameters across the post-redirect.
`hashcards check` now lists byte-identical duplicate cards, naming both file:line locations for each duplicate.

Each grade is now written to the database as it happens, so a session interrupted by a dropped connection or a closed tab keeps the progress made up to that point. Previously an interrupted session was lost entirely.
Bookmark button (shortcut: `b`) during drilling persists cards for later follow-up. Bookmarks survive aborted sessions and can carry an optional note.
Bookmark list at `/collection/{slug}/bookmarks` shows all bookmarked cards with deck name, file path, preview, and note. Orphaned bookmarks (card removed from source) are shown separately.
In-browser card editor at `/collection/{slug}/edit/{hash}`: edits write back to the source Markdown file atomically; FSRS review history is preserved via an in-place hash migration.
MP4 audio files are now supported.
Unified button styles across landing, browse, and completion pages using a shared `.btn` CSS system.
Session completion page now auto-redirects to the collection list after 5 seconds (with countdown and cancel link). Stats are collapsed into a `<details>` element.
Added PWA manifest served at `/manifest.json` (linked via `<link rel="manifest">`) enabling standalone display mode when added to the home screen on supported browsers.
PWA icons (192×192 and 512×512) added and referenced in the manifest, completing Phase A of offline/installable support.
Browse page now has a session limit selector (All / 10 / 20 / 50 cards) next to the Drill button for quick commute-length sessions.

Per-card review time is now tracked: each card's duration (from Reveal to grade) is stored as `duration_ms` in the reviews table. The session completion page shows median pace and the slowest card (deck + duration).
Wrapper button colors (landing, browse, completion) simplified to flat black-and-white; colored drop-shadows and blue accents removed.
Added `serve` subcommand for running hashcards as a persistent web server with multiple collections synced from a git repository.

Added HedgeDoc source support in serve mode: publicly accessible HedgeDoc notes can be used as collections. Sources are managed via a web interface at `/hedgedoc` and persisted to the TOML config file. Syncing follows the same polling interval as git.

Term-definition shorthand: a `T:`/`D:` line pair expands at parse time into two reciprocal front-back cards ("Define: X" and "Term for: Y"). The generated cards hash identically to hand-written equivalents, so review history is preserved when converting. Note: lines beginning with `T:` or `D:` are now card tags, like `Q:` and `A:`.

Review intervals now get a small random jitter (default plus or minus 5%) to diffuse review peaks over time. Configurable via `--jitter` on `hashcards drill` and the `[defaults] jitter` key in the serve config; set to 0.0 to disable. (FEAT-05)

Added a one-line installer (`install.sh`) that downloads, checksums, and installs the latest release binary. Release archives are now published with a `.sha256` checksum file alongside them. Every merge to master that has unreleased changelog entries now cuts a release automatically.

changed.change: Internal cleanup: removed the unused session start time parameter threaded through the drill action handlers, a leftover from the era when reviews were flushed in a batch at session end. (BUG-09)

The database now records its schema version in a `schema_version` table, and schema changes are applied as numbered, ordered migrations instead of ad-hoc column probes. Databases created by newer versions of hashcards are rejected with a clear error instead of being modified. Existing databases are adopted automatically. (BUG-32)
Update dependencies.

The `serve` subcommand no longer requires a TOML config file. Collection directories can be passed as arguments for local use without git syncing. Added `hashcards.example.toml` documenting the config format.
`hashcards stats` now defaults to JSON output. Requesting `--format html` is an error (it was never implemented and previously printed a note to stderr while exiting successfully).

added.change: Added installation instructions to the README.
Publish hashcards on `crates.io`.
Added support for Markdown tables and syntax highlighting of code blocks.
Added button tooltips.
Added a `--host` flag.
Start testing on macOS and Windows.

changed.change: Update dependencies.
Update bind address to `127.0.0.1`.
Put KaTeX into source control.

fixed.change: Fix a bug in the parser that broke TeX math in cloze deletions.
Fixed TeX rendering of matrices.
Fixed TeX math rendering.
Added support for escaping square brackets in cloze deletions.
Fixed button visibility bug on iOS Safari.
Fix card content being invisible with Javascript disabled.

added.change: Added `--answer-controls` flag to the drill command with values "full" (default) or "binary". Binary shows only "Forgot" and "Good" buttons, mapping to FSRS Again and Good ratings.
Added a flag to turn off sibling burial.

fixed.change: Improved the look of blockquote elements.
Improved font selection on Linux.

added.change: KaTeX is now bundled with the executable, allowing hashcards to work entirely offline.

changed.change: Cards are shuffled randomly at the start of a session.
Update dependencies.

fixed.change: Fix a bug where the card cache was not cleared on undo. See [PR #57](https://github.com/eudoxia0/hashcards/pull/57).
Fix the initial flicker when rendering TeX math.

breaking.change: BREAKING: Media file paths are now deck-relative instead of collection-relative by default. Use the `@/` prefix for collection-relative paths.
BREAKING: Flashcards can no longer reference external URLs (e.g., `https://...`) in media file paths.

added.change: Deck files accept TOML frontmatter, so you can override the inferred deck name.
The session completed page shows a button to shut down the server.
Flashcards can be separated using `---` as an explicit separator.

changed.change: Killing the server with `ctrl+c` at the end of a session causes the server to die with exit code 0.
SQLite is once again bundled into the binary, increasing the executable size but reducing build problems especially on NixOS.

fixed.change: Flashcards can reference external URLs.

added.change: Add extra metadata to `Cargo.toml`.
Add `pre-commit.sh` hook.
The `macros.tex` file now supports comments: lines starting with `%` are ignored.
Add CSS to render `blockquote` elements in a grey box.
The `drill` and `check` commands now validate that images/audio files referenced in flashcards actually exist.

changed.change: The UI now works on small and mobile viewports.
Update dependencies.
Update KaTeX to `0.16.25`.

fixed.change: Fixed a bug where exclamation marks broke the parsing of Cloze deletions. See [issue 29](https://github.com/eudoxia0/hashcards/issues/29).

added.change: Added `CHANGELOG.xml`.

changed.change: SQLite is no longer bundled into the binary, reducing the executable size.
